newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Palestinian women celebrate, some fear future.
newsitem.headline: Palestinian women celebrate, some fear future.

text.p: Released Palestinian women prisoners celebrated their first day of freedom on Wednesday but some worried about returning to traditional Moslem families who consider jail a social stigma.

Israel late on Tuesday released 30 women from its jails under a peace deal it signed with the Palestine Liberation Organisation in 1995. They were received by Palestinian President Yasser Arafat in the West Bank city of Ramallah immediately after their release.
One other woman was supposed to be freed on Wednesday.

The reunions with families were emotional: they hugged, kissed and wept. Some mothers ululated with joy as their daughters got off a bus which carried them from jail to Arafat's headquarters in Ramallah.
The women flashed victory signs as they came off the bus at 2 a.m. (2400 GMT) and fell into the arms of loved ones.

But they all said freedom was bittersweet because they were unhappy their colleague, Lamia Maarouf, a 32-year-old Brazilian citizen, was deported to Brazil. They also lamented leaving behind other prisoners. Palestinian sources say around 5,000 Palestinians remain in Israeli jails.
Houses of the women's families were crowded with people who arrived to congratulate them on their first day of freedom. Most received heroe's welcomes.
One woman was worried about life with her conservative family who considered her imprisonment a stain on the family's honour: "I don't know how I will return to live with my family now."

Lawyers at a human rights organisation who visited the woman in jail said she comes from an extremely conservative family and was unhappy at home. They refused to give details for fear of prompting family retaliation against their daughter.

Some very conservative families, who bar daughters from leaving their parents' homes unchaperoned unless they move to their husband's houses, view their daughters' imprisonment as a blot on the family's honour.

In protective Middle Eastern societies, a woman who spent time in prison has few marriage prospects. Often a woman who shames the family, usually by committing adultery, is killed or forced to marry a relative or an elderly man.

"After our release, we expect to be greeted by society and our families as heroes, but we know we are constrained by traditions and habits in our eastern society," said another freed prisoner, Aisha Abu Hamed, 23, who was arrested in 1995 for stabbing an Israeli soldier in Jerusalem.
"Not all families accept the fact that their daughters go to jail," she told Reuters, saying her family found it difficult to cope with her out of the house and in jail.

"If the woman is strong and determined, she might be able to convince her family of the situation," she said. "Anyway once the family visit their daughter in prison and realise there are other women in jail with her, they are forced to cope with reality."
